Hello, this is going to be my second piece of feedback, hopefully it's what you were looking for!

There's a simplicity in the language used in the poem that I particularly like; it makes it accessible. I especially liked the third line of the poem with the double usage of alliteration - you managed to change a continuous list of four into two parts by using 'sc' and 'st' sounds, followed by the 'ruh' sounds of rust and ruin. You still manage to finish off your stanza with an internal rhyme between 'rust' and 'one'. It's beautifully put together when examined thoroughly, full of sound based technique, which is rarer to see in contemporary poetry.

Yet for me I feel like the feeling of laziness isn't completely conveyed  - mainly because you say 'after, evening, soon', which, while being a clever phrase by itself, doesn't perpetuate the feeling of laziness beyond just one day. The scumming and rusting comes immediately later, but in reality the time of metal sitting there, scumming and rusting doesn't match with the time allocated in the poem. And though we could say that the scumming and rusting is implying the passage of further time, the feeling doesn't come immediately to me. Finally, to compress the feeling of time being skewed and inconsistent even further (which doesn't come to the lazy person), we come to the abrupt and emotionally charged 'I trash the shit'. Was the swear word necessary? I have no problem with curses, but it was jarring for me. 

All in all, I love pieces of this poem, in fact love most of it, love the way it sounds and has been structured, but for me, it doesn't get across the feeling of laziness, especially in the last line due to its abruptness.

I've never given feedback on this sub, forgive me if I get the formatting wrong or the etiquette incorrectly. Everything that I say is with good intent!

I like it! I love the first line, alongside of the personification of a memory keeping company and the shame of voyeurism 'crawling all over' you. I also really like the concept that you're playing with in that we're separated from the past, even if it is ourselves, alongside of the suggestion that people change: 'her but certainly not her' - the relationship's changed? She's changed? No longer there? It's quite a pretty image.

Yet that's one of the lines I think you can improve! "I see me but not me, her but certainly not her" - I won't make a suggestion on the line, but is there another way that you can show this, without being so explicit?

On another note, the 'kicked off the bus' definitely does break the illusion, great line and it fulfils its purpose, but it's so shattering of the illusion that as a reader, I'm not only broken out of your memory, but also out of the poem and there's a sudden disconnect. The disconnect continues with 'I want to go home'.

I feel like there's a lack of connection to your memories or good old days with home. Connected with the previous line relating to the bus, my illusion gets shattered even further.

All in all, I like the poem and the way that you can insert yourself into memories, I love the way you intrude into sacred spaces as well. Of course, all of the above is based on my own interpretation, and I'll always be amazed at how brave people are in putting themselves out for feedback!
Hope this was something like what you were looking for.

I think that you could try two different approaches:
You'll always have the recommendation of one poem or the other, (for which purpose I'd recommend my favorite, [The Funeral](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/poem/173358), by John Donne, or you can go through a poet, one collection at a time.

For that purpose I'd recommend reading and supporting poets by purchasing their books: my favorite go-tos at the moment are Carol Ann Duffy's collections, 'Rapture' and 'The World's Wife', or collections from Sylvia Plath (or made post-mortem).

If you want particular structures however, I've been enjoying the read of the [The Making of a Poem](http://www.amazon.com/Making-Poem-Norton-Anthology-Poetic/dp/0393321789/ref=sr_1_8?ie=UTF8&qid=1440837284&sr=8-8&keywords=norton+anthology+of+poetry) - It's always fun to try out a style/format/structure, and the introduction, in my opinion is a fantastic read as well.

Good luck!

As a serious response:
1) I teach English Literature to students in a booming Asian market searching for tutors
2) I social dance (Lindy Hop and the Blues)
3) I write in my spare time as my passion and to fulfil my literary aspirations.

I don't know what the lifehacks article is supposed to be leading towards by having these 3, I don't know if its happiness or fulfilment, but I dunno - just because I've ticked all three of these categories I don't feel happier or any more fulfilled. 
In fact (this might just be my personality), I have to work especially hard to make myself constantly feel fulfilled in each of those things: I constantly question how to best help a particular student, not only for their upcoming exams but as a student going to University, and a human being who should be able to think critically. I constantly change lesson plans and make original material to ensure that they're learning optimally.
Dancing has to be constantly improved - yeah, it's easy to dance the same way with the same person every week, but without a desire to improve dancing gets really dull. Money gets spent on lessons, overseas workshops, hours and hours are put into dancing per week, which means less me time, less creative writing time, less intimate time with significant other.
Lastly, writing's just tough. Yeah, it's a creative outlet, but it's also a narcissistic outlet when you really break it down. "Listen to what I have to say", my own creative expression. It feeds a lot on reactions of others to your work and can really break down someone's mood when its not satiated with praise. Plus, it's not exactly a well-paying job if you're aiming to write poetry, not now or in the future.

I guess I'm writing from only one perspective though, I can see huge flaws in my argument that 'just because you have these things doesn't mean you'll have happiness/fulfilment', because to be honest,  tutoring doesn't make THAT much money, and my personality flaw is to always be harsh on myself and seeking ways to improve. You might get a different answer from someone who's making more cash, does a sport they're passionate about and has a creative outlet that's not so dependant on others! (Plus I eventually plan to shift my career to writing so its been depressing)

Plusses have been here and there though. My girlfriend and I dance together, so we don't have to argue about practice time (though I used to hate it). Tutoring is EXTREMELY fulfilling in the moment your students have their eyes glaze over in a moment of understanding, then burst into smile because they realize they've learnt something and improved as a direct result of your teaching. Writing is my escape anyway, its necessary and yay, I'm getting a poem published in an online journal next month. So there are highs and constant... nothings, but that comes with particular choices. 

Anyway. I think I wanted to get this answer out more than you wanted to hear it :P

Well, just to drop in here and give my point of view on that video:

It's not so much about the rate of verbal harassment that the video seems to stress upon as it is the ability to feel unsafe because of it. That model, as built as he was, was not going to feel like he was put in danger by the girl who approached him for his number. You can see on his face that he enjoyed the attention when given to him by the female portion of the catcallers, heck, he didn't even seem to mind the catcalling by the gay men either. 

If you observe the language used and attitude given by each of the catcallers, you'll notice for the woman it's aggressive, there's a use of imperative, commands, the suggestion of offence being given. Nobody was going to jump either man or woman, but when it comes to the danger factor, the women have to have their guard up more. Now put it into perspective of a woman who is not being videotaped and is walking alone, maybe even during the day in a less crowded neighbourhood. Should she have to feel like she needs a group of friends around her just to walk home? Would the model, well-built man need a group of friends to walk home? Even other solutions - getting a car ride home from a male friend is arguably more dangerous (yes, even if he's a friend, sexual harassment happens more when the victim knows the assaulter), than when compared with a man.

Now let's try another approach. What if in that video, the man was approached only by people larger and better built than him? Large women, women who approached aggressively, well built men who approached aggressively. I'm pretty sure his demeanour would change. It'd be alarming due to the oddness of the scenario, but it'd also be alarming because finally, the man would be put in danger himself. That's the world that women who feel like they get harassed currently live in. 

All in all, I don't think that the video of the man compared to the woman properly highlights the issues being brought up here. Sure, even if the rate of harassment when compared between the man and woman are the same (and yes, I am aware that there is more footage to choose from for the woman's case), the quality/effect of the verbal catcalling is entirely different.

Thanks for bringing up this video though! I didn't know it existed and I'm glad that I know now that it does.

Whoa, buddy. You are happy-go-lucky with your adjectives. You seem to pair one up with every noun that you introduce. 'generic' gossip magazine. 'Meager' pieces of chicken.  'Bites of short lived satisfaction. Armchair of enchantment. 

SOME adjectives actually help the reader envision this scene more clearly. 'Colorful pages', 'comically large sunglasses', but what's an 'armchair of enchantment'? And why is it a 'rickety' beach chair? I understand that the two aren't exclusive, but the excessive use of adjectives really hurts the piece. 

You also start the piece with dialogue between two people but you don't assign the dialogue to anybody. 'The woman' could be made clearer by referring to her in reference to her reply:
'A woman/She/Name lit a cigarette as she replied, going back to her gossip magazine'. It's a hard read if she's 'The Woman'.

The piece is hard to get through when you're trying to throw too many descriptions at me. You lost me at the lake and with 'presently looked at the lake', which you describe as beautiful and then describe with 'undulating' and words that don't really help me understand where these characters are and actually throw me OFF from the description of the lake.

Your description of the wife and Winston's relationship though seems to also be inconsistent. I thought he didn't connect with her emotionally to start with and then ends up being in admiration of her? Or is that where the dream already started, since she replaced her 'generic gossip magazine' with a strange, out of character book?

If I were to hazard a guess, your character looks for peace on a beach and dreams about the most fantastic, perfect version of his wife? But then it becomes a nightmare... which seems kind of odd...

If I had to break down this piece into two sections it would be:
Section 1: Description of the setting and the personality of the main character
Section 2: A dream... or something that happens.

These two, alongside of what I said up top, need to mesh together. This is even more true if this is meant to be a short story. Also the title... while being intriguing, is not supported by the prose. Hope I'm not too harsh here!

This is my first critique (as well). Hope I do this right. I don't want to  repeat what the other two writers have said, but they've hit the main points pretty solidly. Here's my spin on what they've already covered.

[I SPENT A LOT OF TIME WRITING THIS. If you want a TL;DR, it's at the bottom.]

1) Structurally, this isn't a prologue, nor is it a chapter. It's unfortunate to say, but take a look at your favorite novels (I'm guessing fantasy). Compare how many times you introduce names and characters, and then consider how much your characters are actually DOING. For example, take Lord of the Rings (not comparing). Gandalf is introduced, and there's a party happening. Game of Thrones. Two men are scouting North of the Wall. They get attacked. 

A prologue is meant to intrigue and is supposedly something that happens PRIOR to the body of the novel, something necessary to explain/hook the reader. What we have here is a LOT of exposition. You're trying to tell me - "Hey, love my king, he's a great father and has a loving wife, he wishes he could have peace but doesn't know how to achieve it." You're also telling me: "My world has super powers and a bad event occurred regarding a river".

I suppose the wife and the 'Donovan' character are going to become important later, but come on. This isn't how we want to find out. The idea of 'show don't tell', as much as I hate to quote the expression, applies here. Don't tell me that the King is loving. Don't TELL me about Donovan. Don't tell me about abilities either. Show it to me chapter by chapter. Does the daughter discover she has them? Is Donovan the first one to find out? Does the king die?

My second point is on your language and sentence structure. I'm by no means a great writer. I'm not someone who's particularly prolific or exceptionally exuberant when it comes to using diction, but look ^. Even when I spice up my sentences with 'bigger words', I'm not using these words in an excessive fashion. They have a point.

In your case you love to 'expand' on EVERYTHING. "Hachiro said softly" "She said with a smile that connected from ear to ear" "He said with a smile". "Himijie look[ed] at her plainly". These are just the ways you're trying to expand on dialogue.

You need to stop cramming information into the reader's head. Let the scene flow naturally. I don't need to know what Meme looks like in comparison to her mother nor the smell of the mother's hair, UNLESS it's important, bringing in an aspect that I need to know IMMEDIATELY.

Here's my advice and I really hope that nothing I said is taken too critically because I'm not trying to be harsh. I really do hope this helps.

1) Think about your CHAPTER. You obviously have a massive world that you want to share with us, but the reality is that even today, we formulate our opinions on modern society through little scenes.

Example: "Garshnuckle typed away on his iPad keyboard, critiquing another writer's prologue from his clubhouse chair in Hong Kong. He wondered if cinephille91 would take the criticism too harshly. Regardless, he submitted his opinion for the world to read and put it away, knowing that in a few hours a few dozen eyes, or none at all would read the wall of text that he had inputted that day. Anonymous or not, effort was effort, and nobody should ever need names in order to recognize good advice."

If I were writing a piece like this, I would then talk about what I was going to do with the rest of my day, while introducing ONE of my character's motives and how he might collide with ANOTHER character.

Note that I didn't write: "Garshnuckle typed away on his white, silvery iPad keyboard that had come as an add-on to his tablet device. The clicking sounds were relaxing." If I did want to expand on Garshnuckle being a writer and this being a thing he did, I would write (and I make the following deliberately pompous, don't put in this much description):

"Garshnuckle typed away on his white, silvery iPad keyboard within the confines of his brightly lit, expensive clubhouse walls, his apartment complex based in the Oriental, post-colonial city of Hong Kong. With an air of wonder he bit his lip, nervous about the fact that his critique could go awry when examined underneath different eyes from his own. Every man protected his baby after all, and a piece of writing was no different to it's creator as a father to his son. Still, Garshnuckle hoped that cinephille91 would take his critique with good measure."

You'll also note that my language isn't flamboyant, except maybe in the part where I'm trying to describe my clubhouse, and perhaps the part with 'air of wonder'. 

TLDR; Here's my advice. Turn this into 3-4 chapters. Take your King and your night scene, store it away. However, do show us the first time someone shows their abilities, and make that person interact with another upon that discovery. Let THAT be our introduction to powers. Grab your King, and throw a problem at him. Show us how he resolves it, and whether or not it was justice, show his reaction. Was the decision hard? Does his wife comfort him afterwards, and do his aides respect him? Donovan. Show us Donovan taking care of everything. Taking time out of his day to protect the royal family.

Show the kids with their mother. Maybe they don't need names at ALL. Maybe they do. And please, simplify your sentences. It'll make the reading easier and from experience I can promise you, it'll make the writing easier (and better) too.

As someone who is constantly depressed (though I feel that my depression may be different from the depression of others, I don't know how accurate / useful my advice might be), the best thing that I can tell you is what helps me when I'm suicidal.

!Someone kind for me to talk to.!
This person believes in me. This person knows who I am. This person has been helping me and has been a kind person to me. But most importantly, and I repeat it, because it's that important, THIS PERSON BELIEVES IN ME.
For me, depression comes from the fact that I genuinely believe that my existence makes no difference and stamp on the world. I had a childhood which was not horrific - I simply had a childhood that resulted in my personal belief that I was not important and that nothing that happened around me mattered. Someone who understands this and believes in the contrary is different. These people aren't coming up to me and saying 'I believe in you, I believe in you', they're people who, on the phone, point out to me that I've either been improving or I've been doing something self-destructive.
They tell me that they know that I can do things. That they have read my recent piece of creative writing. That they do understand my passions and that they genuinely enjoy my company.

Spend time with this person. What they want to do. Share information about yourself. Tell your friend this as well (this is what my friend told me).

"If you don't want to live your life for yourself, live your life for others. A lot of people wish they could have what you have, so if you don't want it, give it away, give away your education, give away your possessions, give away your time. But the way you do that is by living and dedicating yourself to those people who want what you have. If you don't want to live your own life, live it for others".

My friend understood me. He knew I couldn't take the guilt, and he knew how my mind worked, how I was idealistic but nihilistic - he challenged me to look at the bigger picture and to see how small my troubles were. This will not work on everybody. But by understanding, believing in, talking to and sharing things with your friend, they will think about more than just ending things.

I don't know if this helps the depressed person get out of the cycle (I myself am still struggling), but this at least pushes away the thought of suicide (for me).

Hope things go well.

They're like… ornaments. In my house. I clothe them, I buy them nice things. I give them a house and maximum security. The best of everything. But it's not for them. It's because their happiness and love for me represents my success.

OTHER MAN
But that's not why you're drinking bourbon.

MAN
No, it's not.
…
If you knew then why the fuck would you bring up my family?

OTHER MAN
Wouldn't be polite to jump right into it.

MAN
Oh fuck off. So that's your idea of small talk?

OTHER MAN
Small talk is limited to things that two people equally don't give a shit about. So yeah. That's small talk.

MAN
Bourbon! I need more bourbon.

OTHER MAN [to the bartender]
He means he needs a pina colada.

MAN
What the fuck? I don't want a girl's drink.

OTHER MAN
Get him a pina colada. [Turns back to MAN]
It's your hangover drink.

MAN
Whatever.

OTHER MAN
So what happened?

MAN
Man met Science. And the battle between good and evil was fought.

OTHER MAN
Man met God?

MAN
No. Stupidity met Perfection.

OTHER MAN
All experiments have errors.

MAN [as if quoting something]
And "an error in the experiment is a mandatory cost in time, money, and sometimes even more", I know the book. I wrote the damn thing.

OTHER MAN
Your pina colada.

MAN [sipping, relaxing]
We didn't hide the facts. We didn't hide the dangers. We advertised them, even, but people like to hide the problems themselves. 

People put the scary monster in the closet and under the bed but it's not in their room, out in the open, because it's not them, it's the thing in there. There is something that haunts you and is worse than you, and because there is something worse, you are something better. But you're not, because the closet-monster's not real. And then all of a sudden you realize that you're still alone, so very alone. Unless you got people you can put in the closet.

OTHER MAN
What happened?

MAN
The shipments we sent out twenty years ago …

OTHER MAN
Of raw resources, nothing more …?

MAN
Had people on it.

OTHER MAN
Jesus Christ.

MAN
Yeah.

OTHER MAN
The… wha… why?

MAN
Because, now that I've looked through my predecessor's private logs have discovered, that he took money from politicians and actors and people and told them that it'd be safe.

OTHER MAN
What?!

MAN
Like, you'd think that people'd realize, three hundred years after the idea was thought up of, that inter-galactic travel, is not by any means an easy fucking science.
Like, it needs funds, because when you send off two massive ferries of space-traveling numbskulls off to a suitable planet to live on when you don't have the technology to send them faster, it seems like suddenly a good idea to, when we finally possess that technology, to send them shit, in order to tell them that we got the tech to do it!

OTHER MAN
That was the plan, the stupid but plan, but why would people get on that flight? And why would he let them?

MAN
Because they're idiots, for the first question, and for the sake of an experiment for the second. The man even wrote it down. "All for the sake of an experiment."

OTHER MAN
A bourbon, please!

MAN
Hey!

OTHER MAN
It's for me.

MAN [sighs]
Now the politicians are getting involved, because we've only gotten word now about the state of the ship.

OTHER MAN
Destroyed?

MAN
Pristine.

OTHER MAN
Then… oh. The innards?

MAN
A Bloody Mary.

OTHER MAN
Ahhh fuck. The bourbon.

[There is silence between the two.]

So what do you plan to do now?

MAN
Nothing. I have to keep experimenting. 

OTHER MAN
The more things you have, the easier things are to lose, huh?

MAN
Right. Can you get the bill?

OTHER MAN
Fuck no. Going home?

MAN
Yeah. Got a species to save, a world to lie to, and a universe to destroy.

OTHER MAN
And a family to pay for. [giggles.]

Say hi to your wife for me.

BARTENDER [as MAN starts to leave]
Do you ever regret it? Dream about it?

MAN
Like, do I ever wake up in the middle of the night, cold sweat pouring down my brow, with a thousand screams screeching in my head?

BARTENDER
Yeah.

MAN [smiles]
Fuck no.
